sources.title: Iwasaki Yatarō (Q380105), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-02): label 'Iwasaki Yatarō', description 'Japanese industrialist; founder of Mitsubishi (1835-1885)', born 1835-01-09, died 1885-02-07, citizen of Japan, Korean label 이와사키 야타로. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Iwasaki Yatarō', Encyclopaedia Britannica (read in full, about 250 words). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: industrial entrepreneur who founded the Mitsubishi zaibatsu, the second largest of the family-owned industrial-financial combines that dominated Japan's economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; began as financial manager of the Tosa fief, transferred the fief's shipping interests into his own concern (named Mitsubishi Shokai in 1873), and in 1884 acquired the government's Nagasaki shipyard, which the government encouraged in order to end dependence on foreign shipping.

'IWASAKI Yataro', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures, National Diet Library, Japan (read in full, about 200 words; biographical note written by NDL staff from standard Japanese reference works). States he took over the Tosa clan's enterprises and founded Tsukumo Shokai, later renamed Mitsubishi Shokai and then Mitsubishi Mail Steamship, that the company handled military transport for the Taiwan Expedition and the Satsuma Rebellion, that it tried mining, shipbuilding, finance and trade, and that it competed fiercely with Kyodo Unyu.

'Chapter 6: Entrepreneurs', Autograph Manuscripts and Original Artwork of Well-Known People, National Diet Library, Japan (read the Iwasaki section, about 300 words). Describes him as a Meiji entrepreneur who traded with Tosa officials, set up Mitsubishi Shokai and held an exclusive right to maritime shipping under government protection, and presents his 1877 letter to Ueno Kagenori noting that Mitsubishi provided the government with 38 ships for military transport. Used for the government-protection point only.

Mitsubishi Corporation, 'Our Roots' series, vols. 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 on Yataro Iwasaki (Mitsubishi Corporation; read through Internet Archive copies of the company site because the live pages refuse automated access; about 2,500 words in all). A corporate history by the successor company with an admiring, heritage tone: his Edo studies and seven months in prison after accusing a magistrate of bribery, the Tosa trading offices in Nagasaki and Osaka, acceptance of the 1874 Taiwan transport, the 1875 Shanghai line and price war with Pacific Mail, salary cuts and the 1876 bonuses, coal, copper and shipyard acquisitions, withdrawals from camphor and yarn, and the company's own commentary on him. Treated as self-interested corporate self-report.

'History of Mitsubishi Group', Mitsubishi Electric (read in full, about 1,000 words). Group-company history that covers the 1870 Tsukumo Shokai founding, the three-diamond emblem, the 1874 Taiwan transport and government gift of ships, the 1875 Mail Steamship name, the Shanghai line, the 1880s government-backed rival and the 1885 merger that created NYK. Corporate source, used for corroboration only.

'Mitsubishi Corporation', International Directory of Company Histories (via encyclopedia.com; read in full, about 3,500 words on the Iwasaki period). Independent business-reference history: peasant-born, bought samurai status, purchased Tsukumo Shokai in 1870, enjoyed Finance Minister Okuma's lobbying, subsidies and privileges, controlled about 80 percent of Japanese maritime traffic by 1877, was attacked in the press for unscrupulous practices and monopoly pricing, drove out a rival in 1881, bought Takashima coal and leased the Nagasaki shipyard, secretly bought a majority of Kyodo Unyu in 1885 and ran Mitsubishi as a family concern with authoritarian control. COUNTER-VOICE source (the edition read is a company-history reference work without a named author on the entry).

Portrait photograph of Iwasaki Yataro reproduced in 'Iwasaki Yataro-den' (Biography of Iwasaki Yataro), vol. 2, edited by the Iwasaki Yataro and Iwasaki Yanosuke Biography Compilation Committee, 1967, National Diet Library Digital Collections (info:ndljp/pid/2976210), shown on the National Diet Library's portrait exhibition page as portrait 3. Used for the portrait only, not for any trait row.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_iwasaki_britannica, src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_ndl_portrait | 1869-1884 | encyclopedia + business reference + corporate history + national library] When the domains were abolished he moved the Tosa fief's shipping business into his own company (Britannica, NDL); he accepted the 1874 Taiwan transport that the government had trouble finding a carrier for and was given ships afterwards, opened the Yokohama-Shanghai line in 1875, bought coal (Takashima, 1881) to secure fuel and then leased the Nagasaki shipyard to secure ships (International Directory of Company Histories; Mitsubishi Corporation; Britannica). The move-by-move sequence is documented in independent and corporate sources, but the openings came partly through government patronage and his friendship with Finance Minister Okuma, so the score reflects exploitation of openings more than pure foresight.

competitiveness.rationale: [src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_ndl_portrait, src_iwasaki_mitsubishielectric | 1875-1885 | business reference + corporate history + national library + group history] A price war with Pacific Mail on the Shanghai line cut fares by more than half and ended with a buyout of Pacific Mail's line (Mitsubishi Corporation); in 1881 Mitsubishi drove the rival Tokyo Fuhansen out of business and then fought Kyodo Unyu in a competition that nearly bankrupted both companies (International Directory of Company Histories, Mitsubishi Electric), and in 1885 he secretly bought a majority of Kyodo Unyu in what the directory calls possibly the first hostile takeover; the corporate history says he hated to lose. Independent, corporate and library sources agree on the pattern. The independent source also reports monopoly pricing and press attacks, which is why the impact is dual-edged. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): competitiveness lowered from 74 / 0.56 to 70 / 0.52 because almost all of the evidence is in company-published histories and only one non-company source is critical.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_mitsubishielectric | 1874-1884 | corporate history + business reference + group history] He accepted the 1874 Taiwan transport despite the risks (Mitsubishi Corporation), sustained a fare war that halved fares and a rivalry that drained both companies of nearly all their resources (International Directory of Company Histories), and moved into coal, copper, shipyards, insurance and railway investment (Mitsubishi Corporation); the same corporate history records that he withdrew from the camphor business after three years of monopoly criticism and from yarn-making when profits fell. The pattern shows large bets with exits when they failed, but the 'despite the risks' framing is the company's, and each bet was backed by state favour, which lowers the risk he personally bore.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_mitsubishielectric | 1870-1885 | business reference + corporate history] The directory says that although Mitsubishi was organized as a company he ran it as a family concern with authoritarian control and that his samurai associates could not act as independent managers until after his death; the corporate history says he and other executives took sharp salary cuts during the Shanghai fight, paid the first company bonuses of about one month's pay in 1876 and founded a merchant-marine school and a business school in the late 1870s. He clearly built and drove an organization, but the managerial picture is two-sided: independent source says centralised control, the company stresses staff development. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): leadership_drive lowered from 70 / 0.52 to 66 / 0.48 because the evidence is company-published history and a business-reference entry, with no independent biography.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_britannica | 1854-1885 | corporate history + business reference + encyclopedia] The company history says he wrote on a shrine gate before leaving for Edo that he would not return until his aspirations were realised, was known among classmates for ravenous study, and said near death that he had accomplished only one or two of every ten things he set out to do; his scale of accomplishment is documented independently (Britannica, directory): a second-largest zaibatsu from a peasant-born start. The ambition anecdotes are company-published and uncorroborated. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 72 / 0.52 because the motive-revealing evidence (shrine inscription, deathbed remark, classmate testimony) comes only from the company's own heritage history, while the independent sources document outcomes rather than drive.

adaptability.rationale: [src_iwasaki_mitsubishicorp, src_iwasaki_directory, src_iwasaki_ndl_portrait | 1870s-1884 | corporate history + business reference + national library] He moved from clan trading office manager to private shipowner when the domains were abolished (NDL, Britannica), adopted new names as the business changed (Tsukumo Shokai, Mitsubishi Shokai, Mitsubishi Mail Steamship), and dropped the camphor and yarn ventures when criticism or profits turned against them (Mitsubishi Corporation); in the 1880s the company turned to coal and shipyards when its shipping monopoly was attacked (International Directory of Company Histories). Documented shifts, but they are described at company level and the withdrawals come from a single corporate source.

portrait.source: Portrait photograph of Iwasaki Yataro (photographer unknown), taken during his lifetime and therefore before 1885, shown as portrait 3 on the National Diet Library (Japan) 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures' page for him (image file 0237_3.jpg, 1529 x 2064 pixels) and drawn from the 1967 'Iwasaki Yataro-den' vol. 2 in the NDL Digital Collections (info:ndljp/pid/2976210). Rights basis: (1) the library's 'About This Site' page, which I read live, states that all images used in this digital exhibition are in the public domain and may be reproduced or reused, including for commercial use, without application to the library, with the source cited; (2) independent of that, the photograph was necessarily taken before the sitter's death in 1885, so its copyright in Japan (photographs under the 1899 Act, anonymous author) expired long before 1996 and was not restored in the United States, and for the United States an unpublished or published anonymous photograph of that age is in the public domain; (3) the 1967 book is only a photographic reproduction of a two-dimensional photograph. Caveats: the photographer and the exact date are not stated on the NDL page (a Commons note elsewhere says the portrait was taken in 1874 citing a Japan Art Archive entry that I could not open, so I record only 'before 1885'); I could not read the NDL's per-image source caption because it is not exposed in the page; the portrait is recorded as a likeness because it is a lifetime photograph of him. Lead check: the lead's initial lead was this same NDL portrait (the 630 x 582 Kokushi Shozo Taisei plate on Commons); I used the larger NDL file of the same sitter instead. File downscaled from 1529 x 2064 to 889 x 1200 pixels, never upscaled.
